T99-01694 
 XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is a 27-year-old citizen of Iran who fears persecution in Iran on the basis of religion (practising Su fi who belongs to a particular sect harassed by the government) and perceived political opi nion. While performing military service with the Seppah Pasdaran he was once detained for four days and given an extra three months extra military service after a dispute with a superior officer. He said he joined the Seppah via a military lottery. He worked in a Seppah-controlled hospital in XXXX as an orderly who helped with injections and bandages. He said he never asked for a transfer from the Seppah because this would have caused more problems. He said he never dealt with prisoners or conducted any medical experiments on them. He said he never participated in killing or torturing people when asked to comment on the Seppah’s reputation for human rights abuses.
1 The Minister’s Counsel intervened in this claim under Article 1F(a) of the Convention i.e. that there were serious reasons for considering the claimant’s involvement in war crimes, crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. The Minister’s Counsel submitted that the Se ppah Pasdaran was involved in murder, extermination, enslavement, deportations and persecution on social and religious grounds. He alleged that the claimant was complicit in crimes against humanity although he never alleged that the claimant was directly involved. He submitted that mere membership in the Seppah Pasdaran was not sufficient to bring the claimant under the ambit of Article 1F(a). He also submitted th at the Seppah could not be said to have a limited, brutal purpose. However, the Minist er’s Counsel suggested instead that the claimant had personal and knowing participation within a shared common purpose. He submitted the claimant was an accomplice who would lend active support to the group. However, the panel finds the claimant to be a very credible witness who provided endless and precise details about his work as a hospital orderly. The panel finds he had no position of leadership and participated in no human rights abuses. Exhibit M-3 
 
1 For example, Exhibits R-5 and M-3 
2000 CanLII 21418 (CA IRB)
T99-01694 
 2 contains contradictory information regardin g recruiting practices for the Seppah. The documentation suggests that the Seppah is st affed by both volunteers and a draft lottery system as attested to by the claimant. Gi ven this contradictory information the panel finds the claimant’s contention of being drafted to be plausible. There is information in Exhibit R-5 that another arm of the Iranian security forces, the Revolutionary Guards, operates five universities. The panel finds it is not beyond the realm of possibilities that the Seppah could run a hospital. What was most impressive about the claimant was his straightforward demeanour and his ability to give spontaneous and detailed answers to countless questions. The panel concludes he was an orderly in a Seppah-run hospital who was not involved in human rights abuses and who served in the Seppah not out of his free choice. The panel finds him to be an extremely consistent and credible witness. The panel finds that the Minister’s Counsel ha s not met the onus of establishing that there were serious reasons for considering the clai mant was involved in war crimes, crimes against peace or crimes against humanity. The panel also concludes in reviewing the documentation
2 that there is no systematic pattern of harassment or discrimi nation directed against Sufi adherents in Iran per se. However, the panel also took into account the claimant’s particular circumstances and the fact that in the country documentation (Exhibits C-2) twelve dervishes linked to the claimant’s type of religious practices were hung in 1996 by Iranian authorities. The documentation also makes clear that the claimant ’s type of Sufi sect could be considered deviant by Iranian authorities (Exhibit R-2). At page 21 it states, “XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, an adherent of the Sufi tradition, reportedly was executed on charges of adultery and homosexuality after a coerced confession in 1996. Sufi organizations outside Iran reported an increasing level of repression by th e authorities of Sufi religious practices.” The claimant gave extremely detailed evidence about his sect’s religious practices and past and present leadership. The panel finds that the claimant was credible in stating that 
 
2 See especially Exhibit R-3

T99-01694 
 3 his Sufi sect was persecuted because of the political beliefs of his XXXX (leader). The panel finds that the claimant faces a serious possib ility of being persecuted should he return to Iran. For all the above reasons, the pane l determines XXXXXXXXX to be a Convention refugee. “XXXXXXXXXXXXXX”
